newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FEATURE - Ivory Coast tackles female circumcision.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ivory Coast tackles female circumcision.

text.p: At 12, Vivianne Die had reached puberty and among her Yacouba people of Ivory Coast that meant the time had come to prepare for marriage.

One misty morning, Vivianne entered a shack knocked together in the back of their thatched-roof village. Well-built aunts pinned the girl down while another woman, selected for her age or expertise, sliced at her genitals with a crude knife without any sterilisation or anaesthetic.
"Anytime now she must be given into marriage," said her father, 51-year-old Bernard Die. "That is the tradition. No respectable man is going to marry her unless she is circumcised."
Cutting off of a woman's clitoris, which eliminates most of her sexual pleasure, is widely termed female circumcision -- to opponents of the practice it is simply genital mutilation.

"It was painful but I had no choice since, without it, I was not going to get a husband," Vivianne said during a ceremony in her village in the northwest of Ivory Coast when she and a dozen other girls who went through the ritual were presented to the public.
"Now, I can stand and be respected by prospective suitors."

Vivianne is one of thousands of girls who go through the controversial ritual in the West African country of 14 million people each year. According to Minister for Women and Family Affairs Albertine Herpie Gnanazan, at least four million Ivoirian women have been circumcised.
AUTHORITIES JOIN CAMPAIGN AGAINST PRACTICE
After years of protests by women groups who call it a human rights abuse, authorities have decided to throw their weight into a campaign against the practice.
It is invariably carried out in unsanitary conditions in the bush and complications -- sometimes leading to death -- include tetanus or later problems with childbirth.
But the national committee formed in October to educate adherents on those health risks faces strong traditions.

Coming of age ceremonies abound in traditional African societies, often involving tests of endurance such as ritual flogging of Fulani boys in northern Nigeria. Supporters say female circumcision, often laden with spiritual significance, is is necessary for hygiene and to curb promiscuity by denying a woman sexual pleasure.

The practice occurs in varying degrees across sub-Saharan Africa. In Sierra Leone, where activists say about 90 percent of women are circumcised, it is aggressively defended by the secretive Bondo women's society.
A 28-year-old Sierra Leone woman, Daphne Pratt, said in October she was forcibly circumcised by a gang of Bondo women who seized her at night and accused her of spying on their ritual.

"There is no way we are going to make any progress eradicating the practice without seriously examining the spiritual aspects, which the rural communities hold dear," said Ivorian human rights lawyer Matthew Biley Boua, a lecturer in law at the National University of Abidjan.

"We all agree female circumcision is bad and should be stopped, but what most anti-circumcision campaigners are not aware of or do not acknowledge is that there are things involved which the ordinary eye cannot see."
PLAN TO RECONCILE TRADITIONS

Maire-Guy Bah Kone, a 63-year-old practioner, who put away her tools five years ago after 40 years of cutting young girls, is trying to reconcile those traditionals in her role as coordinator of Ivory Coast's national campaign.

"Circumcision has traditional values and beliefs among all the tribes who practise it," she said. "There are unseen forces involved which must be pacified so that they would not bring havoc on the people if circumcision is stopped."
She does not elaborate on how the gods can be appeased, but she has asked authorities for funding that could pay for rituals which normally involve the sacrifice of large numbers of animals.

Yai Constance, president of the Ivoirian Association for the Defence of Women's Rights, likes the plan to show peasant farmers a more humane way to please the spirits than cutting up girls at puberty.
"What we are doing is to convince those who believe in the practice to substitute an animal in the place of slicing the genital of the teenage girl," she said.

"As for the rest of the initiation, during which girls are taught various things about the new society they are about to enter, we have nothing against it since it does not involve any human rights abuse."
